newsitem.title: CAMEROON: Cash injections up in Central Africa franc zone.
newsitem.headline: Cash injections up in Central Africa franc zone.

text.p: Central Bank cash injections into the Central African CFA franc zone rose in February for a third consecutive month on continuing strong demand to fund commodity marketing seasons, the bank said.

Interbank market activity showed a marked increase for the first time since November 1996, as Cameroonian banks returned to the scene after a one-year absence, the Banque des Etats de l'Afrique Centrale (BEAC) added in its monthly bulletin.
Total volume of transactions on the monetary market increased by 36.8 percent to 31.6 billion CFA from 23.1 billion in January.
February saw four tenders for a total of 92.6 billion CFA, amounting to an average weekly injection of 23.1 billion per tender, compared to 12.8 billion in January.
Chad accounted for 81.9 percent of the Central Bank's global bank financing, compared to 8.8 percent for Congo, 7.2 percent for Central African Republic and 2.4 percent for Cameroon.

"In Chad, banks drew more on the Central Bank due to the enormous volume of finance needed for the cotton marketing season. Funds doubled between January and February, going from a daily average of 8.6 billion to 17 billion," the bulletin said.
On the interbank market, total transactions registered 6.3 billion CFA in February, more than double January's 2.7 billion.

The bulletin said two transactions took place on Cameroon's interbank market -- one between a national and foreign bank for five billion CFA for a duration of 28 days with an interest rate of 5.44 percent, one a regional transaction between two institutions in the same group for one billion CFA for a period of 28 days at 7.75 percent. Gabon was the only other country to register any activity on this market.
The average interbank rate in February went up slightly to 5.833 percent, from 5.415 percent in January, due to a dip in banks' treasury surpluses.

Global bank deposits at the BEAC also rose in February, although there was a variable trend according to each country. Deposits for the zone averaged 75.2 billion CFA in February, up from 64.8 billion CFA in January.
Banks in Cameroon retain the highest average daily deposit rate, but this decreased slightly in February at 30.7 billion CFA, against 32.4 billion CFA in January.

Bank deposits in the Central African Republic, still trying to recover from its third army mutiny in less than a year, decreased in February to 1.6 billion CFA from 2.4 billion in January and 4.4 billion in December. Banks there channelled reserves into funds for cotton marketing and oil purchases.

Gabonese banks again increased deposits, which reached 34.2 billion CFA, against 23.8 billion in January and 21.2 billion in December, as they received advance repayments on loans granted to oil companies.
The BEAC indicative money market rates were unchanged with the intervention rate at 7.75 percent and the two to seven day lending rate at 9.75 percent.

The Central African monetary zone groups six countries in the region -- Cameroon, Central African Republic, Congo, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea and Chad. ($1=577 CFA francs) -- Clare Black, Abidjan newsroom +225 21 90 90
